title: On tiptoe
hook: on tiptoe you can't stand firm; striding, you won't go far (Tao Te Ching 24)

segments.voice: Yesterday, chapter twenty-three: the whirlwind that can't last a whole morning, and your line was speak little. Where did you say less, and what filled the space? A new week starts here. Day one thousand eighty-six.

If you're standing, try this. If you're sitting, just imagine it. Rise up onto your toes, as high as you can. For a second you're taller. Then the calves start to burn, the ankles wobble, and your arms go out to the sides looking for balance. You can't stay there. You can't walk well like that either. Come back down, and feel the whole foot take the floor again: heel, arch, toes. That's steadiness, and it cost nothing. Chapter twenty-four of the Tao Te Ching starts right there, with a person straining on their toes.
screen: `RISE ONTO YOUR TOES.` → `THE WOBBLE.` → `COME BACK DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, tiptoe, not firm. In Legge's translation the chapter begins: "He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm." The extra height is borrowed. It has to be paid back, and quickly. Second, striding, not far. The next line says the same of walking. Whoever stretches their legs into long strides won't get far. A person who lunges down the road wears out before someone who just walks. The chapter is about posture, but not only about feet. Third, chapter twenty-two, in reverse. Two days ago, chapter twenty-two said the sage doesn't display himself, and so he shines; doesn't boast, and so his work counts. Chapter twenty-four turns the same lines inside out. Whoever shows himself off isn't seen clearly. Whoever insists he's right doesn't stand out. Whoever boasts gets no credit. Whoever is proud of himself doesn't last. Showing off, in this picture, is a kind of standing on tiptoe: you look taller, and you can't hold it. Fourth, leftover food, a growth. Then comes a blunt image. To the Way, the chapter says, these straining habits are like leftover food, or a useless growth on the body. Things people turn away from. So whoever has the Way doesn't stay in them. It isn't a moral scolding so much as a diagnosis: the strain is extra. It weighs on you and gets you nowhere. Flat feet, the whole sole on the ground, is the steadier way to stand.
screen: `TIPTOE, NOT FIRM.` · `STRIDING, NOT FAR.` · `CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO, IN REVERSE.` · `LEFTOVER FOOD, A GROWTH.` · then, large: `HE WHO STANDS ON HIS TIPTOES DOES NOT STAND FIRM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop straining at one thing. Sit with both feet flat on the floor, and feel them there. Now bring to mind one place in your life where you're up on your toes: trying to look like you have it handled, pushing a project faster than it can go, keeping up with someone. Don't solve it. Just let your weight come down into your feet, and ask what it would look like to stand on the whole foot in that one place. The bell holds the time.
On tiptoe. Chapter twenty-four's picture of strain: taller for a moment, never firm, and a stride too long to last. Today's word.
Your line: flat feet. When you catch yourself straining today, to impress, to hurry, to win, feel your feet on the ground and come down off your toes. Day one thousand eighty-six.

howItsDone: Some people who read the Tao Te Ching use chapter twenty-four as a check on themselves: when they notice strain or showing off, they come back to a plain, steady way of standing and working.

myth: chapter twenty-four is only advice about how to stand
it starts with feet, then turns to showing off, boasting and pride.
chapter twenty-four turns chapter twenty-two's lines about the sage inside out
twenty-two: he doesn't boast, so his work counts. twenty-four: whoever boasts gets no credit.
the chapter says long strides get you there faster
whoever stretches into long strides won't get far.

fork.setup: you want to look taller than you are, for a moment, in a crowd. chapter twenty-four is watching. what happens on tiptoe?
options: you can hold it as long as you need.
you can't stand firm, and you have to come down.
you grow into the extra height.
fork.reveal: "he who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm." the height is borrowed, and the chapter says the same of showing off.

original.note: Chinese, qǐ zhě bù lì: one on tiptoe does not stand. The opening of Tao Te Ching 24.

trapdoor: what you thought: on tiptoe is about being careful and quiet.
what it means: straining to be taller; you can't stand firm that way, and showing off works the same.
what a scholar hears: qi zhe bu li, the tiptoer doesn't stand, and a chapter that mirrors twenty-two, calling the strain leftover food and a useless growth.

sources.quoted: He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm

sources.ref: Tao Te Ching, chapter 24 (long strides; showing off, self-justifying, boasting, pride; leftover food and an excrescence)
Tao Te Ching, chapter 22 (the mirrored lines)

notes: Verify the Legge 1891 wording: 'He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm'.
The rest of chapter 24 is paraphrased, including 餘食贅行 rendered as 'leftover food, or a useless growth on the body' (Legge: 'remnants of food, or a tumour on the body'). Confirm.
The tiptoe exercise in the hook is offered as optional ('if you're standing... if you're sitting, just imagine it') for accessibility.
Day 1085 closes the previous week; this day opens a new one.
